We wanted to build a management layer that could sit beside ClickHouse® rather than inside it.

That led naturally to two decisions:

Use the interface ClickHouse® already provides.

Package the management application into the smallest practical deployment artifact.

HTTP gives CH-Ops a clean network boundary.

The compiled executable gives CH-Ops a clean deployment boundary.

SQLite keeps the application's state independent.

And the absence of agents keeps the ClickHouse® cluster untouched.

So the real architecture is surprisingly simple:

Install CH-Ops somewhere
        |
        v
Give it persistent storage
        |
        v
Give it network access
        |
        v
Point it at ClickHouse®

No CH-Ops agent to distribute across the cluster.

No separate frontend service required for the production build.

No Node.js installation required on the target machine for the compiled binary.

No requirement for CH-Ops to become part of the ClickHouse® server.

That is what lightweight by design means to us.

Not fewer features

event_model_payload.headline: Freeze a Flake Only After a Clean Runner Reproduces the Same Class
event_model_payload.summary:
A flake freeze is a recorded exception, not a pass. An agent patch may receive that exception only after a second runner, started from a clean workspace, reproduces the same failure class on the same fixture hash and the same minimized input. One local red bar is not enough. Agreement is the evidence; disagreement closes the freeze lane.

Agent diffs fail in ways a single log line collapses. The property can be false. The fixture can have drifted. The test can be flaky, or the machine that wrote the patch can be dirty. Those cases need different dispositions. A merge gate that treats every red as a freeze candidate will hide deterministic bugs, while a gate that treats every red as a hard blocker will also stall on a known flake the patch never touched.

Decision matrix

The matrix below is a policy, not a measured benchmark. Rows are exhaustive for the fields the packet records. No timing data and no pass-rate claim sits behind it.

Local class Clean-runner class Property cohort Freeze lane
flake-shaped same class, same fixture hash pass eligible
flake-shaped pass pass refuse; environment miss
flake-shaped different class any refuse; unstable signature
deterministic any any refuse; fix or revert
any unavailable any refuse; fail closed
flake-shaped same class fail refuse; property owns the bug

Read the last two rows as hard stops. A missing clean run is not a waiver. A failed property cohort is not a flake, even when both runners print a similar stack.

Why runner identity is a field

The authoring workspace is a biased sample. It holds editor swap files, a warm dependency cache, a partial environment file, and whatever the agent wrote while iterating. A rerun on that machine often repeats the bias. Calling the second local rerun confirmation double-counts one environment.

Runner identity has to be coarse enough to audit and fine enough to detect reuse. A useful id is the image digest plus a workspace nonce generated at job start, not a hostname alone. Hostnames collide in autoscaled pools. Nonces that persist across jobs also miss the point of the field.

If the two ids match, the vote is a refuse. The clean runner must also echo the fixture hash it actually loaded. A log that says replayed without that echo is an incomplete run, and incomplete runs take the unavailable row.

Prerequisites, not the thesis

Earlier gates already constrain eligibility: shrink the failing input first, pin the fixture hash, reject a looser bound, and do not mint a new freeze token merely because a property check went green. This article does not reopen those rules. It adds a constraint they do not express. A locally perfect packet can still be an artifact of the authoring machine.

Treat those earlier checks as inputs to this vote. If shrink did not run, do not set local_class to flake_shaped. Leave the class empty and let the checker refuse.

Numbered workflow

  1. Pin identities before any rerun. Record patch_hash, test_id, fixture_hash, minimized_input_hash, and oracle_version. If any field is empty, stop. A freeze without those keys cannot be audited on the next patch.

  2. Classify the local failure into a closed set: flake_shaped, deterministic, or environment. Map assertion-text edits and bound edits into deterministic unless a separate waiver record already exists. Do not add a fourth class inside the runner script to force a green vote.

  3. Run the property cohort on inputs the suspected flake does not own. The cohort must pass on the candidate patch. A pass here does not authorize a freeze. It only shows the patch did not break the unrelated invariant set you chose to lock.

  4. Start a clean runner that did not author the patch and does not reuse the local workspace, dependency cache, or editor scratch files. Replay only the minimized input against the pinned fixture hash. Store the remote class, the remote fixture hash, the remote input hash, and the remote runner id.

  5. Compare, then persist. Eligibility requires equal failure class, equal fixture hash, equal minimized-input hash, a passing property cohort, a completed clean run, and two distinct runner ids. Write packet.json first. A second command consumes the packet and either prints eligible or a refuse reason. Do not fold that decision into a YAML conditional that nobody reviews.

  6. Expire the packet when oracle_version or patch_hash changes. A new patch is a new vote, even when the test name matches a freeze that was valid yesterday.

Property cohort and clean replay may run in parallel. The vote waits for both. A fast property pass must not short-circuit a missing clean run.

Build the runner id in the job, not by hand:

nonce=$(openssl rand -hex 8)
image=$(docker image inspect "$CI_IMAGE" --format '{{.Id}}' 2>/dev/null || echo "local-uncontainerized")
printf 'img:%s+nonce:%s\n' "$image" "$nonce" | tee runner.id
sha256sum fixtures/locked.json cases/minimized.json | tee packet.hashes
git rev-parse HEAD > packet.patch_hash

The local-uncontainerized fallback is honest, not a pass. Two jobs that both print that fallback still need different nonces. If you cannot name the image, say so in the packet and keep the refuse path easy to hit.

Reference checker

The module below is a proposal. This draft does not report an execution against a production suite. The function encodes the vote. It does not discover flakes, shrink inputs, or talk to a network.

from dataclasses import dataclass

ELIGIBLE = "eligible"
REFUSE = "refuse"

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class FreezeVote:
    test_id: str
    patch_hash: str
    fixture_hash: str
    minimized_input_hash: str
    oracle_version: str
    local_runner_id: str
    clean_runner_id: str
    local_class: str
    clean_class: str
    clean_fixture_hash: str
    clean_input_hash: str
    property_cohort_passed: bool
    clean_run_completed: bool

def decide(vote: FreezeVote) -> str:
    required = (
        vote.test_id,
        vote.patch_hash,
        vote.fixture_hash,
        vote.minimized_input_hash,
        vote.oracle_version,
        vote.local_runner_id,
        vote.clean_runner_id,
    )
    if any(not field for field in required):
        return REFUSE
    if not vote.clean_run_completed:
        return REFUSE
    if vote.local_runner_id == vote.clean_runner_id:
        return REFUSE
    if vote.local_class != "flake_shaped":
        return REFUSE
    if vote.clean_class != vote.local_class:
        return REFUSE
    if vote.clean_fixture_hash != vote.fixture_hash:
        return REFUSE
    if vote.clean_input_hash != vote.minimized_input_hash:
        return REFUSE
    if not vote.property_cohort_passed:
        return REFUSE
    return ELIGIBLE

Expected results, if that module is imported as written, are assertions rather than a claimed CI history:

def test_vote_matrix():
    base = dict(
        test_id="prop_balance_holds",
        patch_hash="c0ffee",
        fixture_hash="abc123",
        minimized_input_hash="def456",
        oracle_version="oracle-7",
        local_runner_id="img:sha256:1111+nonce:local",
        clean_runner_id="img:sha256:1111+nonce:clean",
        local_class="flake_shaped",
        clean_class="flake_shaped",
        clean_fixture_hash="abc123",
        clean_input_hash="def456",
        property_cohort_passed=True,
        clean_run_completed=False,
    )
    assert decide(FreezeVote(**base)) == REFUSE
    base["clean_run_completed"] = True
    assert decide(FreezeVote(**base)) == ELIGIBLE
    base["clean_runner_id"] = base["local_runner_id"]
    assert decide(FreezeVote(**base)) == REFUSE
    base["clean_runner_id"] = "img:sha256:1111+nonce:clean"
    base["clean_fixture_hash"] = "drifted"
    assert decide(FreezeVote(**base)) == REFUSE

A synthetic packet shows the on-disk shape. The hashes are placeholders, not an incident report.

{
  "test_id": "prop_balance_holds",
  "patch_hash": "c0ffee",
  "fixture_hash": "abc123",
  "minimized_input_hash": "def456",
  "oracle_version": "oracle-7",
  "local_runner_id": "img:sha256:1111+nonce:local",
  "clean_runner_id": "img:sha256:1111+nonce:clean",
  "local_class": "flake_shaped",
  "clean_class": "flake_shaped",
  "clean_fixture_hash": "abc123",
  "clean_input_hash": "def456",
  "property_cohort_passed": true,
  "clean_run_completed": true
}

Load it only after the hash files exist:

python - <<'PY'
import json, pathlib
from freeze_vote import FreezeVote, decide
raw = json.loads(pathlib.Path("packet.json").read_text())
print(decide(FreezeVote(**raw)))
PY

Suggested process exits, if you wrap decide in a CLI: 0 when the result is eligible, 2 when a required field is empty, 3 when classes or hashes disagree, 4 when the clean run did not complete. Keep the mapping in one module. CI should call the module, not reimplement the table.

Where drafts and a clean workspace fit

Property statements still have to be written, and a model draft is not a verdict. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. MonkeyCode's free model access is relevant as a drafting aid: request candidate invariants from the patch diff, then discard any draft that is not executable or that restates the assertion under test. decide never reads a confidence score. It reads hashes, classes, and a boolean the cohort runner computed.

The free server option is relevant as one way to obtain clean_runner_id. Use it as an isolated replay workspace for the minimized case and, if policy allows, the property cohort. Persist the remote fixture hash or refuse the vote. A remote status of success without that hash is still the unavailable row. Nothing here states a quota, a hardware shape, a time limit, or a promise that the option remains free.

Keep packet.json in the repository that owns the merge. A remote log is an input to the vote, not the record of record.

If a second isolated workspace already exists inside the network, point clean_runner_id at that workspace and do not send fixtures anywhere else. The vote depends on distinct runner identity and matching hashes, not on who operates the second machine.

Limitations

Two runners can share a bug. The same base image, the same clock-skew window, or the same external stub will reproduce a false flake twice. Dual agreement raises the bar. It does not prove the failure is nondeterministic in production, and it does not estimate a flake rate.

Non-reproduction is ambiguous. A clean pass means not attested, not that the local failure was imaginary. Retrying until the clean runner fails manufactures eligibility. Cap the clean attempt at one replay of the minimized input. A second try requires a new packet and a written reason field that decide currently ignores on purpose, so a human has to widen the schema knowingly.

Seeded tests only. The policy assumes the minimized input and the fixture hash fully determine the case. UI timing tests, live network calls, and unordered thread dumps do not meet that assumption. Do not coerce them into flake_shaped to make the table close.

The reference checker does not parse pytest, JUnit, or vendor CI logs. Adapter code is separate work. An adapter that drops clean_fixture_hash while still marking clean_run_completed true will hide the gap only if someone later deletes the hash check. Do not delete it to green the pipeline.

Shared image digests are a residual risk, not a reason to skip the nonce. Record both. If you cannot rebuild the clean workspace from the same lockfile as CI, the run is not clean, and the vote should refuse even when ids differ.

Who should not use this

Skip the approach when the case cannot leave the private network and no internal clean runner exists. A shared or public workspace is the wrong place for secrets, customer fixtures, or vulnerability-adjacent inputs. Fail closed instead of redacting logs ad hoc and hoping the class string survived.

Skip it when the suite has no minimized input. Replaying a long full-fixture job on a second machine copies cost and hides the failing bytes. Shrink under the existing rule, or do not freeze.

Skip it when a freeze is expected to mean this red is accepted forever. The packet expires with the patch hash and the oracle version. Teams that need a standing waiver need a different process, with a human owner on the record and a review date. This checker will not invent that owner field for you.

What to merge

Merge when the property cohort passed and the freeze lane was either unused or eligible. Do not merge on a local red the clean runner did not confirm. Do not merge when the clean runner was skipped to save minutes.

Store the packet beside the test for the life of the waiver. The next agent patch should fail this vote until it produces its own attestation, even if the test name matches a previous freeze. That is the point of binding the exception to patch_hash rather than to the test title alone.

event_model_payload.headline: Building a Secure AWS VPC with EC2: A Hands-On Networking Lab
event_model_payload.summary:
Launching an EC2 instance is a great starting point for learning AWS, but real cloud environments require more than virtual machines. We need network segmentation, controlled access, routing, and a secure way for application components to communicate.

In this hands-on project, I worked on an AWS VPC and EC2 lab that brings these concepts together.

The environment includes public and private subnets, route tables, security groups, an OpenVPN server, a Squid forward proxy, an NGINX reverse proxy, a Windows frontend, and a Linux backend API.

The objective is to understand how these components work together and how to troubleshoot connectivity between them.

🏗️ Architecture Overview

The project uses a dedicated VPC with separate public and private subnets.

  • Public subnets: Host selected components that need public connectivity.
  • Private subnets: Host application workloads without direct public IP exposure.
  • Internet Gateway: Enables internet routing for eligible public-subnet resources.
  • Route tables: Control where network traffic is sent.
  • Security groups: Restrict inbound and outbound traffic.
  • OpenVPN: Provides a VPN-based administrative access path.
  • Squid proxy: Handles configured outbound web requests from authorized clients.
  • NGINX reverse proxy: Routes incoming requests to the frontend or backend.
  • Frontend EC2: Runs a Windows-based web application.
  • Backend EC2: Runs a Linux-based API.

Project architecture: public and private subnets, EC2 workloads, routing, and security controls.

1. Create the VPC and Subnets

Create a VPC named DEV-VPC with this IPv4 CIDR block:

10.0.0.0/16

Private subnets

Subnet CIDR
DEV-EC2-PvtSubnet-01 10.0.1.0/24
DEV-EC2-PvtSubnet-02 10.0.2.0/24
DEV-EC2-PvtSubnet-03 10.0.3.0/24

Public subnets

Subnet CIDR
DEV-EC2-PubSubnet-01 10.0.101.0/24
DEV-EC2-PubSubnet-02 10.0.102.0/24
DEV-EC2-PubSubnet-03 10.0.103.0/24

For a multi-AZ design, place the subnets across different Availability Zones where possible.

Remember: a subnet is not automatically public because of its name. Its route table and the resource's public addressing must support the intended connectivity.

2. Configure the Internet Gateway and Route Tables

Create an Internet Gateway named DEV-IGW and attach it to DEV-VPC.

Create a public route table named DEV-PublicRT with this route:

  • Destination: 0.0.0.0/0
  • Target: DEV-IGW

Associate it with the public subnets that require internet routing.

Next, create DEV-PrivateRT and associate it with the private subnets.

Private instances that need outbound internet access require a suitable egress design, such as a NAT Gateway or a controlled proxy. Do not add a direct Internet Gateway route to a private subnet as a substitute for that design.

3. Configure Security Groups

Create security groups according to each component's role.

Security group Purpose
MyIP-Access Administrative access from a trusted public IP
Squid-Access Proxy access on TCP 8888
Web-Access Required web and reverse-proxy traffic
Frontend-Access HTTP access to the frontend from approved sources
Backend-Access API access on TCP 7000 from authorized components
Remote-Access Administrative access through the approved management path

Security best practices:

  • Restrict SSH (22) and RDP (3389) to trusted sources.
  • Allow only the required OpenVPN port and protocol.
  • Limit Squid access to authorized clients.
  • Allow backend port 7000 only from the component that needs it.
  • Avoid exposing administrative ports to 0.0.0.0/0.
  • Review both security-group rules and the relevant network routes.

4. Deploy OpenVPN

Launch an Ubuntu 22.04 EC2 instance in a public subnet and configure its required public connectivity. Use an Elastic IP if a stable public IPv4 address is needed.

The lab's deployment script is available here:

OpenVPN deployment script

Review the script before running it. Follow its setup instructions and configure the client using the appropriate OpenVPN profile.

After connecting, test access to the private resources permitted by your routes and security groups. VPN access should not mean unrestricted access to the entire VPC.

5. Deploy Squid Proxy

Squid acts as a forward proxy for configured outbound HTTP and HTTPS requests.

The lab provides this deployment script:

Squid deployment script

Review the script and its expected parameters before execution. The example configuration uses the VPC CIDR 10.0.0.0/16.

Configure the proxy to listen on TCP port 8888, and restrict access to approved clients. Never leave a proxy openly accessible to the internet.

For private instances, use the Squid instance's actual private IP when configuring the proxy endpoint.

6. Configure the NGINX Reverse Proxy

NGINX provides an entry point for incoming application requests and forwards them to the correct service.

In this lab:

  • HTTP port 80 serves the frontend path.
  • TCP port 8080 forwards API requests to the backend on port 7000.

The backend proxy destination follows this pattern:

proxy_pass http://BACKEND_PRIVATE_IP:7000;

Replace BACKEND_PRIVATE_IP with the backend instance's private IP address.

Validate the configuration before reloading NGINX:

sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx

Confirm that the reverse proxy can reach the destination and that the destination's security group permits the traffic.

7. Deploy the Windows Frontend

The frontend runs on a Windows EC2 instance in a private subnet.

Repository:

Testing Frontend

The example IIS application directory is:

C:\inetpub\testingfrontend

Follow the repository's deployment instructions to configure IIS.

The instance does not need a public IP for normal private application operation. Use the approved management path for administration and restrict inbound web traffic to the intended source.

If the application calls the API directly from a user's browser, ensure that the API endpoint is reachable from that browser. Use HTTPS for production, and configure CORS where required.

8. Deploy the Linux Backend API

The backend runs on an Ubuntu EC2 instance in a private subnet.

Repository:

Testing API

The lab's deployment script is available here:

Backend API deployment script

Review the script and prerequisites before executing it.

If the backend needs outbound package downloads, configure the intended egress path. For a Squid proxy, the endpoint follows this format:

http://SQUID_PRIVATE_IP:8888

Replace the placeholder with the actual private IP address.

Verify that the backend API listens on TCP port 7000 and is reachable from the authorized reverse-proxy path.

9. Test the Complete Application Flow

Validate the environment one layer at a time:

  1. Check subnet and route-table associations.
  2. Confirm that the public route table points to the Internet Gateway.
  3. Verify that private resources have no unintended public exposure.
  4. Test VPN connectivity and permitted private-resource access.
  5. Confirm that the backend can reach Squid if required.
  6. Test connectivity from NGINX to the frontend and backend.
  7. Open the frontend through the intended entry point.
  8. Test API requests through the reverse proxy on port 8080.
  9. Review NGINX, operating-system, and application logs if requests fail.
  10. Remove unnecessary security-group rules after testing.

Testing each layer separately helps identify whether a failure is caused by routing, security groups, proxy configuration, or the application itself.

What I Learned

This project reinforced several important AWS networking concepts:

  • Subnet segmentation: Public-facing components and private workloads should have clearly defined roles.
  • Routing vs. security: Route tables determine network paths; security groups control permitted traffic.
  • Forward vs. reverse proxies: Squid manages configured outbound requests, while NGINX routes incoming requests.
  • Private-instance access: Private workloads still need a secure management and software-update strategy.
  • Systematic troubleshooting: Checking routes, ports, security groups, and service health individually makes debugging easier.

Security and Cost Considerations

Even a learning lab should follow good security practices.

Use least-privilege access, review remote scripts before execution, keep administrative access restricted, and delete resources when the lab is complete.

Remember that EC2 instances, Elastic IP addresses, NAT Gateways, data transfer, and operating-system licensing can generate charges. Monitor costs throughout the exercise.

For production, consider HTTPS, centralized logging, patch management, highly available entry points, and a documented strategy for secure administration and private-subnet egress.

Final Thoughts

Building a VPC and EC2 environment is about more than launching virtual machines. It is about understanding how routing, network segmentation, access controls, proxies, and application services work together.

This lab is a useful hands-on exercise for cloud learners, AWS certification candidates, and aspiring DevOps engineers who want to strengthen their practical networking skills.

What would you improve in this architecture for a production workload? I'd love to hear how you approach secure administration, private-subnet egress, and reverse-proxy design in your AWS environments.

AWS #CloudComputing #DevOps

event_model_payload.headline: Capturing coding sessions while the desktop app is closed
event_model_payload.summary:
Current stage: Windows desktop development build. Updated 10 October 2026.

A memory app that must stay open throughout every coding session adds another thing to remember. Mind Palace separates the capture process from the desktop interface.

Approved Codex hooks invoke a small local receiver. The receiver writes an inbox record without needing the Angular UI or the vault worker to remain open. When the user opens the vault, the app validates and imports those captures.

The current demo exercises this path with a synthetic hook event and fictional messages. It uses the real packaged receiver and native vault. It does not show a live Codex model producing the conversation.

Keep the hook's job small

The synchronous hook path validates bounded input and writes one unique atomic spool record. It does not scan memory folders, run inference or take the app's shared operation lock.

Moving indexing out of the hook reduces competing work during a short client deadline. It does not remove every timing risk. A receiver still has startup and filesystem costs, and actual client delivery must be measured separately.

App-side indexing validates the spool records and deduplicates deliveries. It publishes content-addressed transcript chunks and ordered manifests. Chunk boundaries follow complete JSONL records; the target is 64 KiB. An indivisible record can exceed that target within the separate input-record limit.

The receiver's complete transcript bound is 20 MiB. Oversized or ambiguous data is reported and preserved rather than advertised as a successful complete import.

Consent must name the source

Capture starts from an explicitly selected transcript folder. History is a separate action: the user reviews source metadata and confirms import. Installing a hook file is also separate from reviewing and trusting that handler in Codex.

This separation prevents several misleading states. A file on disk does not prove the client ran it. A successful capture does not prove the entire history was imported. A saved source does not prove its contents are an approved decision.

Changed hook definitions need fresh client review. The app's setup checklist makes runtime approval uncertainty visible.

Recovery without inventing completeness

Mind Palace can repair missing tails for already known sessions from the approved Codex source folder. Canonical ingestion maps one provider/session identity to one Session, preserving selected source revisions rather than rewriting the originals.

That recovery is useful, but it should not be confused with complete event delivery. A controlled two-minute test recovered an exact source and passed stored-evidence answering while its strict event-count check remained at 18 of 20. The discrepancy remains recorded instead of being replaced by another run that happened to pass.

Retention has a similar boundary. Old prefixes become eligible for cleanup only after a validated vault import acknowledgment and complete reference checks. Unknown, divergent and unimported copies stay intact. A large cleanup scan can defer without deleting anything.

What I would measure before calling capture dependable

  • Whether the client actually loads and trusts the handler.
  • Whether capture works while the desktop app is closed.
  • Whether restart imports exactly the stored source without duplicate Sessions.
  • Whether forced exit and missed-tail recovery preserve evidence.
  • Whether failures remain visible and uninstall restores the expected configuration.

The repository contains measured synthetic native checks and separate installed-client fixtures. They are evidence for their specific paths, not a guarantee for every machine or every future session.

Read the code

Mind Palace is a Windows desktop development build using Angular, Tauri and bundled Python. Claude Code end-to-end verification and public installer work remain separate from the current Codex workflow.

See the repository, the receiver, the inbox implementation and the recorded native results.

If you have built a lifecycle-hook integration, which failure was hardest to reproduce? Share the behavior and a non-sensitive reproduction through repository issues.

event_model_payload.headline: AI Agent Decision Logs: Record Evidence Without Storing Chain of Thought
event_model_payload.summary:
An agent can update a customer record, trigger a refund, or route a support case while every dashboard stays green. Then someone asks the only question that matters: why was this action allowed, and what actually changed? A trace may show tokens and latency. An application log may show an HTTP 200. Neither is a dependable answer.

The missing piece is an AI agent decision log: a small, structured record for each meaningful choice. It links the task, the bounded evidence, the policy and release in force, the chosen action, and the independently verified outcome. It is not a transcript, and it should not be a hidden-reasoning archive.

This guide shows how to build that record so an engineer can debug an incident, an operator can review a risky action, and a customer-data team does not inherit a second copy of every prompt.

A trace is not a decision record

Keep both. They answer different questions.

Artifact Best for Usually misses
Trace latency, retries, spans, model calls business intent and policy verdict
Tool log request/response diagnostics whether the response changed the target state
Prompt release manifest which behavior bundle was deployed why this request took this branch
Decision log why the system was allowed to act and what was verified low-level performance detail

Suppose a support agent changes a renewal status. A trace can show update_subscription completed in 180 ms. A useful decision log can say that the request came from an authenticated account owner, the account was eligible under renewal-policy-v4, the action stayed below the risk threshold, the expected version was 27, and the billing API confirmed version 28 with the requested status.

That is enough to investigate and reproduce the decision without pretending that a model's private intermediate text is a reliable audit artifact.

Record decisions, not every model turn

Logging every token is expensive, risky, and noisy. It also makes review harder. Define a decision boundary: log when the agent crosses from interpretation into a consequential branch or side effect.

Good boundaries include:

  • selecting a workflow or an external tool;
  • classifying a request into an approval or risk tier;
  • changing a record, sending a message, or charging money;
  • denying an action because policy blocked it;
  • escalating to a human;
  • declaring a long-running task complete.

Do not make a decision log for each retrieval chunk, retry, or sentence of a draft. Put those in traces and link their stable IDs when they matter. A compact log should be readable when an incident is active.

Start with one question

Before adding fields, ask: Could a teammate who was absent reconstruct the reason, authority, and result of this action from this one record?

If the answer is no, add the missing reference. If the answer needs the full prompt, full customer record, and every generated token, redesign the workflow so the record can cite safe, scoped evidence instead.

A practical decision-log schema

The schema needs stable identities, not a giant JSON blob. Here is a TypeScript shape for a material action:

type DecisionLog = {
  id: string;
  occurredAt: string;
  tenantId: string;
  runId: string;
  decision: "route" | "allow" | "hold" | "block" | "complete";
  task: { type: string; requestRef: string };
  release: { manifestId: string; model: string; policyVersion: string };
  evidence: Array<{ kind: string; ref: string; sha256?: string }>;
  action?: { tool: string; targetRef: string; idempotencyKey: string };
  policy: { verdict: "allow" | "hold" | "block"; reasons: string[] };
  outcome: { state: "verified" | "rejected" | "unknown"; resultRef?: string };
  redactionVersion: string;
};

Three choices matter here.

First, requestRef, targetRef, and resultRef point to access-controlled data; they do not copy it. A support transcript or invoice belongs in its existing system with its existing retention rules.

Second, store versioned identifiers for the release, model, and policy. An answer may be acceptable under one policy version and blocked under the next. Without IDs, you cannot explain a historical decision honestly.

Third, store the verdict and its public reasons, such as account_owner_verified or refund_below_limit. Do not store a fabricated summary of hidden reasoning. Design the policy engine to emit explicit reason codes that are safe to expose to operators.

Capture evidence before the action, then verify after it

The safest shape is a two-phase record. Write a planned decision before an external side effect; append the verified result after it.

async function changeRenewal(input: RenewalInput) {
  const decision = await decide(input); // typed facts + deterministic policy
  const record = await decisions.insert({
    ...decision,
    outcome: { state: "unknown" },
  });

  if (decision.policy.verdict !== "allow") return record;

  const result = await billing.updateRenewal({
    subscriptionId: input.subscriptionId,
    expectedVersion: input.version,
    idempotencyKey: record.action!.idempotencyKey,
  });

  return decisions.appendOutcome(record.id, {
    state: result.version === input.version + 1 ? "verified" : "unknown",
    resultRef: `billing-event:${result.eventId}`,
  });
}

Why not write the record only after success? Because a timeout, worker crash, or duplicate retry is itself important. The planned record gives you a durable idempotency key. The outcome distinguishes attempted, verified, and unknown instead of silently turning uncertainty into success.

For high-risk actions, send hold records to an approval queue. The reviewer should see the task summary, safe evidence links, policy reason codes, expected change, and expiry. Their approval becomes another append-only event, not an edit to history.

Keep private data out of the log by default

A decision log can become a data leak if it stores raw prompts, retrieval text, tool arguments, or secrets. Use a privacy budget as deliberately as a token budget.

Store directly Store by reference or hash Never store in the decision log
policy version, verdict, time, action type request ID, document ID, sanitized evidence hash API keys, access tokens, raw passwords
model and release IDs encrypted artifact location full hidden reasoning
idempotency key, result status redacted tool-response reference unrestricted customer transcript

Run a redactor before persistence, and version it. A later investigation needs to know which rule set removed or transformed a field. Do not solve this with a vague instruction like “avoid PII.” Make it a schema rule: only allow-listed fields can enter the decision table.

Also separate read permissions. An on-call engineer may need policy codes and status, while a privacy officer may be the only person allowed to open the underlying request reference. The decision log should remain useful even when its linked artifacts are unavailable to the reader.

Make records replayable without replaying production

Replay means testing whether the same typed facts and policy would produce the same verdict—not firing the live tool again.

Create a replay fixture with:

  1. sanitized input facts;
  2. the referenced release and policy versions;
  3. expected decision, reason codes, and action contract;
  4. a fake tool response or recorded result shape. 
it("holds a renewal change when ownership evidence is missing", async () => {
  const result = await evaluate({
    accountOwnerVerified: false,
    requestedChange: "renew",
    riskAmount: 0,
  }, policy("renewal-policy-v4"));

  expect(result.verdict).toBe("hold");
  expect(result.reasons).toContain("account_owner_not_verified");
});

This is more stable than asking a model to narrate its prior thinking. Keep LLM interpretation upstream, constrained by a typed output schema. Make the consequential verdict deterministic where possible. If the model must classify, capture the allowed label, evidence references, confidence as a diagnostic signal, and the policy that converted the label into an action.

Query records like an incident responder

Good records turn vague questions into bounded queries:

  • “Which policy version allowed this action?”
  • “Did we verify the external change or merely receive a response?”
  • “Which release caused the first hold spike?”
  • “Did a retry reuse the same idempotency key?”
  • “Which evidence reference was unavailable during the decision?”

Build a small operational view around those questions. Show the decision timeline, state transitions, policy reason codes, release ID, and safe links. Do not start with a polished chat summary; start with data that makes a summary checkable.

An especially useful alert is a rising count of unknown outcomes. It catches the uncomfortable middle state: a tool call may have reached the destination, but your service cannot yet prove what happened. That deserves reconciliation, not an automatic retry.

Common failure modes

Logging an unbounded prompt blob

It feels thorough until a customer asks for deletion, a secret appears in context, or an operator needs one fact quickly. Store a constrained summary and references; keep original data in the system responsible for it.

Treating a model confidence score as authority

Confidence is not permission. A high score does not replace ownership checks, spend limits, or a reviewer. Policy should decide whether a classification may become an action.

Calling an HTTP response “verified”

An accepted request can still be rejected later, applied twice, or applied to the wrong version. Prefer a returned version, downstream event ID, read-after-write check, or reconciliation job.

Making the log editable

Corrections are valuable; overwriting history is not. Append a correction event that names the original record, the actor, and the reason. That preserves the investigation trail.

A rollout plan that will not stall the team

Start with one high-value tool action, such as changing a ticket state or creating an outbound message. Define its input facts, risk tier, policy reasons, idempotency key, and verification method. Put the log schema under test before adding a dashboard.

Next, add hold and unknown states. Teams often log only success and failure, but these two states capture the real operational ambiguity. Finally, link the record to your existing trace and release manifest. You get an explanation layer without replacing observability, deployments, or access control.

The result is less glamorous than an autonomous demo, but more useful in production: an agent can act quickly and still leave behind a clear, privacy-aware explanation of what it was allowed to do and what the system proved afterward.

Test the contract in CI

Treat a decision log as an API contract. If a release removes the policy version, changes a reason code, or starts serializing a raw email address, the build should fail before that change reaches production.

Start with three small tests:

  • Schema test: every required field is present and every reference uses an allowed prefix.
  • Redaction test: realistic prompts and tool responses cannot introduce secrets, direct identifiers, or unapproved fields.
  • Transition test: unknown may become verified or rejected, but a terminal outcome cannot be silently overwritten. 
it("does not persist raw customer text", () => {
  const record = toDecisionLog({
    task: { summary: "Email ava@example.com about invoice 8841" },
    policy: { verdict: "hold", reasons: ["human_review_required"] },
  });

  expect(JSON.stringify(record)).not.toContain("ava@example.com");
  expect(record.task.requestRef).toMatch(/^request:/);
});

Use fixtures from incidents and near misses after redacting them. A fixture that proves a duplicated retry preserves its idempotency key is more valuable than a generic happy-path example. When a policy changes intentionally, review the fixture diff as carefully as an application permission change.

One final rule helps with multi-agent systems: assign a parentDecisionId when one agent delegates to another. The child still logs its own policy and result. This lets an investigator follow the tree from a user request to a tool action without merging all agents into one unsearchable transcript.

FAQ

What should an AI agent decision log contain?

Include a stable decision ID, time, task reference, release and policy versions, safe evidence references, policy verdict and reason codes, the planned action, idempotency key, and a verified or unknown outcome. Avoid raw prompts and hidden reasoning.

Are AI agent decision logs the same as observability traces?

No. Traces diagnose execution performance and call paths. Decision logs explain a consequential branch or action in business and policy terms. Link the two rather than forcing either one to do both jobs.

Should an AI agent decision log store chain of thought?

No. Store explicit, reviewable policy reasons and safe evidence references instead. They are more reliable for operations and avoid creating an unnecessary store of sensitive, unbounded model text.

How do I verify an AI agent action actually happened?

Use an idempotency key plus a domain-level confirmation: a returned version, durable downstream event, read-after-write check, or reconciliation process. Record unknown until that confirmation exists.

How long should decision logs be retained?

Match retention to the underlying business process, contractual needs, and privacy policy. Keep the smallest useful record, retain linked sensitive artifacts under their own controls, and test deletion and access rules.

Can small teams implement this without a new platform?

Yes. Start with an append-only database table or event stream, typed schema validation, policy reason codes, and links to existing traces and records. Add specialized tooling only after the basic contract is working.

event_model_payload.headline: Finding coding decisions with exact source quotes
event_model_payload.summary:
Current stage: Windows desktop development build. Updated 10 October 2026.

“Why did we choose SQLite?” is a retrieval question before it is a writing task. If the reason already exists in a coding conversation, I want to read that passage and check who said it.

That is the current Ask workflow in Mind Palace, a local desktop vault for coding conversations. It returns stored evidence rather than generating a new explanation.

Start from the original record

The vault keeps selected conversation sources separately from editable session content. Before returning a saved source, the worker checks its recorded size and SHA-256. If it changed unexpectedly, the read fails rather than quietly serving altered evidence.

For captured Codex sessions, the searchable passages come from known user and assistant message fields. System, developer and tool records remain in the raw source but are excluded from this conversation-search view. They should not masquerade as a user's decision.

This is a useful boundary, not an approval detector. An assistant passage may contain a suggestion. A user passage may contain an abandoned idea. The reader must still inspect context.

A deliberately narrow retrieval algorithm

The implementation extracts distinct search terms from the question. It ignores short terms and a fixed set of common question words. It then scans a bounded inventory of stored sessions and checks their conversation passages.

All retained search terms must match a passage. A source result carries the session identity, title, exact quote, source offsets and snapshot hash. The response contains up to three sources. The displayed answer introduces the closest stored passage; it does not invent a rationale.

In the synthetic demo, the source says:

Use SQLite for the local vault because it keeps storage on the device and needs no database server.

Asking “Why did we choose SQLite?” returns that stored evidence. Opening the source shows the conversation it came from.

This is keyword search, not embeddings, a semantic index or a reasoning model. A synonym can miss. Extra terms can make a query too restrictive. The current implementation scans bounded session data; it does not claim unlimited search scale.

Abstention belongs in the interface

If there are no useful search terms or no matching passage, Ask reports insufficient evidence. That result is preferable to filling a gap with a plausible sentence.

The app also separates capture freshness from stored evidence. Certain known capture failures can leave the existing vault readable. Ask then shows an unsynced warning while searching already stored sessions. An answer from those sessions does not prove the latest turn arrived.

Likewise, the banner “Local vault connected · AI off” describes the running state accurately. Storage and keyword retrieval can work while model inference is absent.

What exact quotes do and do not establish

A quote lets you check the source and distinguish stored text from generated prose. A content hash helps detect unexpected modification. Neither proves the speaker's claim is true, identifies the latest valid decision by itself, or establishes that every client event was captured.

Mind Palace preserves the original source so those questions remain inspectable. Suggestions stay separate from explicit approvals. Summary review does not silently confirm a decision.

Explore the implementation

The project uses Angular, Tauri and bundled Python. Current native checks use isolated synthetic data; this is a Windows development build, not a claim of completed installer or cross-platform acceptance.

See the repository, the retrieval implementation and the user guide.

Which would help your workflow more: finding the exact source quickly, or seeing a generated summary beside it? Feedback on that distinction is welcome through repository issues. Do not post private transcripts.

event_model_payload.headline: Atomic-Chat: Run 100% Offline Local AI Agents and LLMs with Zero Cloud Leakage
event_model_payload.summary:
TL;DR

Atomic-Chat is an open-source local AI workspace and inference engine engineered specifically for running autonomous agents and open-weight models on your personal machine. Built entirely with TypeScript, it eliminates expensive API subscriptions and privacy concerns by running completely offline with native inference orchestration.

Key Features & Architecture

  • 100% Air-Gapped & Offline Execution: All inferences, agent logic, and context storage happen locally on your hardware. Zero telemetry, zero external API calls.
  • Optimized for Agentic Workflows: Unlike typical wrapper UIs, Atomic-Chat includes an inference engine built to handle multi-step agent reasoning, tool use, and structured outputs.
  • Broad Model Compatibility: Seamlessly integrates with modern open-weight LLMs (Llama 3, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek) through optimized local inference runtimes.
  • Full TypeScript Ecosystem: Clean, modular TypeScript architecture makes it trivial for web developers and AI engineers to extend agent capabilities, add tools, or customize the UI.
  • Zero Cost Inference: Maximize your existing hardware (Apple Silicon unified memory, NVIDIA RTX GPUs) without per-token charges or rate limits.

Quick Start

Getting started with Atomic-Chat is straightforward via modern package managers:

# 1. Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/AtomicBot-ai/Atomic-Chat.git
cd Atomic-Chat

# 2. Install dependencies
pnpm install

# 3. Launch the development environment
pnpm dev

Once launched, point Atomic-Chat to your preferred local model provider (e.g., Ollama, llama.cpp, or vLLM) or use its built-in inference runtime to start conversing and orchestrating agents immediately.

Why It Matters

Privacy-conscious engineers, enterprise developers bound by strict NDAs, and builders building agentic systems often hit walls with hosted APIs—whether due to data residency policies, latency, or unpredictable monthly billing. Atomic-Chat bridges the gap between raw low-level inference backends and practical, user-friendly agent applications, giving you total sovereignty over your intelligence stack.

🛠️ Recommended AI Stack & Resources

Supercharge your local and cloud AI workflows with these developer-tested tools:

  • Cloud GPU Hosting: Need to run large 70B+ parameter models that won't fit on your local rig? Spin up cost-effective on-demand GPUs with RunPod starting at just $0.20/hr.
  • AI Code Editor: Build local AI agents and hack TypeScript codebases 10x faster with Cursor, the AI-native code editor designed for rapid prototyping.
  • Production Vector DB & Storage: Scale agent memory and persistent RAG pipelines seamlessly with Pinecone or Supabase.

event_model_payload.headline: How I built a local vault for Codex conversations
event_model_payload.summary:
Current stage: Windows desktop development build. Updated 10 October 2026.

A coding conversation can explain why a database was chosen, which approach was rejected, or what should happen next. The code records the result. The conversation often holds the reasoning.

That is the problem behind Mind Palace: keep coding conversations available locally, then find the original passage when the question comes back.

The question I use in the demo is deliberately small: “Why did we choose SQLite?” The answer is not generated. The app finds a stored message explaining that SQLite keeps storage on the device and needs no separate database server. A source button opens the saved conversation so the reader can check it.

The demo uses fictional messages in a real native app. It demonstrates the storage and retrieval path, not a live model conversation.

Three layers, one local workflow

Mind Palace uses Angular for the interface, Tauri for the desktop boundary and bundled Python for capture, storage and search.

Angular handles the setup checklist, session Library and Ask screen. Tauri exposes narrow, validated native commands and owns the worker processes. Python preserves source revisions, imports captured sessions into a vault and searches those sources.

The flow is:

  1. Choose a local vault and explicitly allow a Codex transcript folder.
  2. Install the app's hooks and review their definitions in Codex.
  3. Let approved hooks write captures to a local inbox.
  4. Open the vault or sync to import sessions.
  5. Search with words from the conversation and inspect the quoted source.

The current capture, storage and search path needs no API key or model call. The application enables no developer analytics or hidden cloud sharing.

Keep sources separate from interpretation

An edited summary should not replace the conversation that produced it. Mind Palace preserves selected source revisions as immutable, content-addressed files. New transcript prefixes can update the canonical session without overwriting older source revisions.

One provider/session identity maps to one canonical Session. Reimporting a capture should not create another copy of the same conversation. Ambiguous or divergent revisions remain visible failures instead of being silently treated as the newest source.

This distinction also matters for decisions. A suggestion is not an approval, and reviewing a summary does not confirm its proposed decisions. The repository keeps those boundaries explicit rather than treating every assistant statement as agreed memory.

What the current search does

Ask performs bounded keyword matching over verified stored conversations. It returns an exact passage with a source reference, or reports that it found no matching evidence. It does not synthesize explanations or provide semantic search today.

That narrower behavior makes the output inspectable. It also has limits: different wording can miss a relevant passage, and a matching passage still needs human interpretation. “I found these words” is not proof that a decision remains current.

What is measured

Recorded native checks cover closed-app capture, restart import, exact-source recovery, local Ask and source opening using isolated synthetic data. A complete 20 MiB source passed capture/import/read with matching SHA-256 in an earlier verification run.

Those results do not make this a finished release. Packaging and broader reliability work remain open, including a recorded 18-of-20 event-delivery discrepancy in a separate controlled Codex test. Claude Code end-to-end support and generated model answers are not current product claims.

Try the interface or inspect the implementation

Mind Palace on GitHub includes a browser sample, source, screenshots and setup instructions. The browser sample is fictional, resets on reload and cannot connect a desktop vault. The native workflow requires a prepared Windows build; the repository's development guide explains that distinction.

Start with the user guide or read the verification record.

If you use coding agents, which past decision is hardest to find again? Describe the problem in a repository issue without sharing private conversation content.

event_model_payload.headline: Do We Still Need DevOps Engineers? Azure AI Is Building the Deployment Accelerator That Changes the Answer
event_model_payload.summary:
The shift nobody is talking about honestly!

For a decade, shipping to the cloud meant a stack of specialist work: Terraform modules, YAML pipelines, PowerShell glue scripts, and one engineer who "knows how the release works."

That is changing quickly. Azure now has AI in every layer of that stack: code, infrastructure, pipelines, and operations. Combined, these pieces make a deployment accelerator: describe what you need, and a platform produces, validates, deploys, and monitors it.

My post below will covers what can be automated today, how to build such a platform on Azure, and what still needs humans.

What can be automated with Azure AI

Area Traditionally done by AI-assisted approach on Azure
Infrastructure code Engineer writes Terraform/Bicep Natural-language prompt -> Bicep/Terraform via GitHub Copilot or Azure Copilot, based on Azure Verified Modules
CI/CD pipelines Hand-written YAML Agent generates GitHub Actions / Azure Pipelines from repo analysis
Environment provisioning Tickets + scripts Azure Developer CLI (azd) templates + Azure Deployment Environments
Policy and compliance Manual review Azure Policy + AI review of IaC before merge
Security scanning Separate tooling Defender for Cloud + GitHub Advanced Security with AI fix suggestions
Cost control Spreadsheet reviews Cost Management data + AI anomaly summaries
Incident response On-call runbooks Azure SRE Agent / Azure Monitor + AI triage
Documentation Rarely done Auto-generated from the code and the deployed state

Architecture: the AI deployment accelerator

Developer request (chat / issue / PR)
|
v
AI Orchestrator (Azure AI Foundry agent)
|
+--> Azure MCP Server (read/act on Azure resources)
+--> Template library (Azure Verified Modules, azd templates)
+--> Policy engine (Azure Policy, Checkov, what-if)
|
v
Generated IaC + Pipeline -> Pull Request
|
v
Automated gates: lint, security scan, what-if, cost estimate
|
v
Human approval (for prod)
|
v
GitHub Actions deploys -> Azure
|
v
Azure Monitor + SRE Agent feed learnings back

Step-by-step: how to build it

1. Standardize first. Create a curated library of approved modules (Azure Verified Modules in Bicep or Terraform). AI is only as safe as the building blocks you let it use.

2. Give the agent tools, not freedom. Use Azure AI Foundry to build an agent and connect it to the Azure MCP Server so it can query and operate on Azure through scoped permissions.

3. Make generation produce pull requests, not deployments. The agent writes IaC and pipeline changes into a repo. Everything flows through Git, so you keep history, review, and rollback.

4. Add automated gates.

  • az deployment what-if or terraform plan on every PR
  • Policy-as-code (Azure Policy, Checkov, PSRule for Azure)
  • Secret and vulnerability scanning
  • Cost estimate in the PR comment

5. Use identity properly. Federated credentials (OIDC) from GitHub to Azure and managed identities everywhere. No stored secrets.

6. Close the loop. Send deployment and runtime telemetry back to the agent so it can suggest fixes, tune sizing, and open remediation PRs.

7. Keep humans on production approvals until you have real data showing the gates are trustworthy.

Example: a prompt-to-production flow

"Create a web app with a SQL database in a private network, dev and prod environments, Key Vault for secrets, and alerts to the ops channel."

The accelerator produces a Bicep deployment, a GitHub Actions workflow for both environments, policy checks, and a cost estimate. A reviewer approves, and it deploys. The first draft takes minutes instead of days.

Do we still need Terraform and PowerShell engineers?

Honest answer: the manual typing of Terraform, YAML, and PowerShell is going away. The engineering judgment is not.

AI is very good at producing the first 80% of IaC and pipelines. It is not accountable for:

  • Architecture decisions: network topology, landing zones, multi-region and DR trade-offs
  • Security and compliance ownership: someone must own the risk
  • Reviewing AI output: generated code can be subtly wrong, insecure, or expensive
  • Platform design: building and governing the accelerator itself
  • Incidents with no precedent: novel failures that don't match any pattern
  • Cost and capacity trade-offs that depend on business context

The role shifts from writing scripts to platform engineering, governance, and AI-assisted operations. Teams that don't need ten script-writers may well need two strong platform engineers. Fewer people doing repetitive work is a realistic outcome. "No engineers at all" is not.

Why this is Azure's moment

Microsoft owns an unusual combination: GitHub (code and CI/CD), Azure (infrastructure), Entra ID (identity), Defender (security), Azure Monitor (operations), and Azure AI Foundry (agents). Few other platforms put the full path from idea to running, monitored workload under one identity and policy model, and AI sits across all of it.

Takeaways

  • Start with standards and templates, then add AI on top.
  • Generate through pull requests, never directly to production.
  • Gate everything with policy, scanning, and what-if.
  • Reskill toward platform engineering, security, and AI orchestration.

The question isn't "will AI replace DevOps?" It's "will you be the one building the accelerator, or the one it replaces?"

What are you automating first? Tell me in the comments.

By - Shivanna Gundanavar (MLOps and Cloud)

event_model_payload.summary:
Airdrops represent a significant opportunity for crypto investors, but tracking them manually is inefficient and prone to error. Building an automated monitor using AI APIs allows you to filter noise, predict eligibility, and notify yourself instantly when new opportunities arise. Here’s how to construct a robust system using Python and LLMs.

1. Data Ingestion Pipeline

First, you need a reliable stream of data. Most airdrop information resides on Twitter (X), Discord, and specialized aggregators like AirdropAlert. Use libraries like tweepy or Discord WebSockets to capture real-time messages. However, raw social media data is noisy. You need to filter for keywords like "airdrop," "claim," "testnet," or specific project names.

import json
from ai_api_client import Client

# Initialize your AI client
ai_client = Client(api_key="YOUR_API_KEY")

# Raw data from social media stream
raw_tweet = "Just finished the testnet tasks for ProjectX! 🚀 #Airdrop #Web3"

# Preprocessing: Extract relevant context
context = {
    "source": "twitter",
    "text": raw_tweet,
    "project": "ProjectX",
    "hashtags": ["Airdrop", "Web3"]
}

2. AI-Driven Analysis

This is where AI transforms raw data into actionable intelligence. Instead of simple keyword matching, use an LLM to analyze the intent and legitimacy of the post. You can prompt the model to determine if the post is a genuine claim announcement, a scam, or just hype.

prompt = f"""
Analyze this crypto social media post: {json.dumps(context)}

1. Is this a legitimate airdrop announcement or claim? (Yes/No)
2. What are the eligibility requirements mentioned or implied?
3. Assign a confidence score (0-100) for legitimacy.
4. Extract any deadlines or "claim windows".

Return the response in JSON format.
"""

response = ai_client.generate(prompt)
analysis = json.loads(response)

3. Practical Tips for Implementation

  • Structured Outputs: Always force your AI API to return JSON. This makes parsing and storing data in a database (like PostgreSQL or MongoDB) seamless.
  • Scam Detection: Train

event_model_payload.headline: I built a 17-agent AI swarm on my phone — here's how
event_model_payload.summary:
I built a 17-agent AI swarm on my phone — here's how

Okay, buckle up. This is a bit of a rabbit hole, but a really fun one. I’ve spent the last few weeks building and running a swarm of 17 independent AI agents, all contained within and operating on my phone. Yes, you read that right. No cloud servers, no expensive GPUs. Just a Pixel 7 Pro and a lot of Python.

This wasn’t about solving world hunger (though, hey, maybe someday!), it was about pushing the boundaries of what’s possible with on-device AI and exploring emergent behaviour within a limited computational environment. It’s a proof-of-concept for what I’m calling “FractalMesh,” a system designed for decentralized, localized AI processing.

Why on-device?

The current AI landscape is dominated by massive models running in the cloud. That's fantastic for powerful applications, but comes with downsides: latency, privacy concerns, and reliance on network connectivity. On-device AI, however, offers a lot of promise. It’s faster, more private, and can operate offline. My phone is essentially a mini-supercomputer just waiting to be tapped. The challenge? Squeezing 17 brains into it.

The Architecture: Agents and the Coordinator

The system is built around a central “Coordinator” agent and 17 “Worker” agents. Think of it like a hive mind.

  • Coordinator: This is the orchestrator. It defines the task, divides it into sub-tasks, distributes those sub-tasks to the Workers, collects their responses, and synthesizes them into a final output. It doesn't do the core processing, it manages it.
  • Workers: These are the specialists. Each agent is designed with a specific, focused role. In this iteration, I've got agents for:
    • Sentiment Analysis (x3): Evaluate text for emotional tone.
    • Topic Extraction (x3): Identify key themes within text.
    • Keyword Generation (x3): Brainstorm related keywords.
    • Text Summarization (x3): Condense text into concise summaries.
    • Question Answering (x3): Answer questions based on provided text.
    • Translation (x2): Translate text between English and Spanish.

Tech Stack & Optimizations: Python, llama.cpp, and a LOT of patience

The core of the project is Python, running via a custom script I’ve packaged with Termux on Android. Termux provides a Linux-like environment on Android allowing me to run Python and install packages. However, running full-blown transformer models (even smaller ones) on a phone isn’t feasible without serious optimization.

This is where llama.cpp came in. llama.cpp is a fantastic project that allows you to run large language models (LLMs) quantized for CPU usage. This is crucial for phone performance. I used a quantized version of the TinyLlama model (1.1B parameters, Q4_K_M quantization) for each agent. It's not GPT-4, but it's surprisingly capable for its size.

Here’s a simplified snippet demonstrating how an agent (let's say a Sentiment Analyzer) is instantiated and used:

from llama_cpp import Llama
import time

class SentimentAgent:
    def __init__(self, model_path):
        self.llm = Llama(model_path=model_path, n_ctx=512, n_threads=4) # Threads adjusted for phone cores

    def analyze_sentiment(self, text):
        prompt = f"Analyze the sentiment of the following text: '{text}'.  Respond with 'Positive', 'Negative', or 'Neutral'."
        output = self.llm(prompt, max_tokens=20, stop=["\n"], echo=False)
        return output["choices"][0]["text"].strip()

# Example usage
sentiment_agent = SentimentAgent("/sdcard/models/tinyllama-q4_k_m.gguf") # Path on phone
text_to_analyze = "This is an absolutely amazing project! I love it!"
sentiment = sentiment_agent.analyze_sentiment(text_to_analyze)
print(f"Sentiment: {sentiment}")

Key Optimizations:

  • Quantization: Using Q4_K_M quantization reduced the model size significantly, allowing me to fit more agents.
  • Context Length: Limiting the context window ( n_ctx in llama.cpp) to 512 tokens helped keep memory usage down.
  • Thread Control: n_threads was set to 4, matching my phone's core count. Experimenting with this value is crucial for performance.
  • Batching: While not fully implemented yet, I'm planning to batch requests to the same agent type to improve throughput.
  • Prioritization: The Coordinator prioritizes tasks and agents based on estimated complexity. More complex tasks get more resources (longer processing time).

The Coordinator's Role: Orchestrating the Swarm

The Coordinator is where the real magic happens. It receives an initial text input, breaks it down, and assigns portions to the appropriate Workers. Here's a simplified view of the Coordinator's logic:

import threading

class Coordinator:
    def __init__(self, agents):
        self.agents = agents  # Dictionary of agent types (sentiment, topic, etc.)
        self.results = {}

    def process_text(self, text):
        self.results = {}
        threads = []

        # Divide the task & assign to workers
        for agent_type, agent_list in self.agents.items():
            for agent in agent_list:
                thread = threading.Thread(target=self.run_agent, args=(agent, text, agent_type))
                threads.append(thread)
                thread.start()

        for thread in threads:
            thread.join()

        # Synthesize results (currently just prints them)
        print("--- Results ---")
        for agent_type, results in self.results.items():
            print(f"{agent_type}: {results}")

    def run_agent(self, agent, text, agent_type):
        # Run the agent's function
        if agent_type == "sentiment":
            result = agent.analyze_sentiment(text)
        elif agent_type == "topic":
            result = agent.extract_topics(text)
        # ... other agents ...

        self.results[agent_type] = result

This example uses threading to run agents concurrently. The actual implementation is more complex, handling error

event_model_payload.headline: How AIClaw 3.7.4 Keeps Generated Images Visible After Reopening a Chat
event_model_payload.summary:
An agent generates a picture, saves it successfully, and answers with a local filename. The tool did its job. The user still has to find the file to see the result.

That was the gap behind AIClaw 3.7.4. The release adds inline previews for generated images, including images restored from older conversations. The interesting part was making the result survive the whole trip through tool execution, storage, and history replay.

AIClaw is an open-source desktop agent with an Electron/Vue interface and a Go kernel. Here is how this change fits into that architecture.

A small UI contract

The display rules are deliberately simple:

  • One image gets a larger preview below the answer.
  • Multiple images appear as a row of thumbnails that wraps when needed.
  • Clicking a preview opens a large image viewer inside the app.
  • Escape, the close button, or a click on the backdrop closes the viewer.
  • The filename remains available as an action for opening the local file.

The images sit outside the collapsed execution steps. A user can inspect the output without expanding the tool log, while the log remains available for understanding how it was produced.

The preview starts with tool metadata

The renderer collects image artifacts from successful tool steps in the current turn. It filters supported image extensions and deduplicates paths within that turn.

The path comes from the tool result's artifact metadata. We do not scan the assistant's answer for anything that resembles a filename. An assistant can mention an example path or describe a file that was never created; that text alone should not become a preview.

The flow is:

Tool execution → artifact paths → saved tool result → restored history item → turn-level image collection → preview

In the Go message structure, the persisted field is small:

// Artifacts are local UI metadata, omitted from model requests.
Artifacts []string `json:"artifacts,omitempty"`

The model request builder omits this field. The UI needs it to restore local outputs; it does not need to add those paths to the model's request payload.

The bug that only appeared in history

A preview working during a live turn is only half the job. Older sessions were saved before artifact paths were included in the stored messages.

Some of those sessions also used Code Mode. The image tool ran inside the exec wrapper, so the outer tool result was a string describing the generated file. That string could be plain text or JSON-encoded text, and it could appear among multiple output lines.

Supporting only the direct image tool missed that case. Reopening the conversation still produced the answer and filename, but no image metadata reached the renderer.

The compatibility path now handles the standard saved-image result emitted by both generate_image and exec. For wrapper output, it attempts to decode each line as a JSON string before matching the known result format.

This is intentionally narrow: it recognizes the tool's standard Chinese or English success prefix and its generated image filename format. It keeps existing structured metadata when present, deduplicates recovered paths, and avoids extracting files from arbitrary assistant prose or unrelated tools.

That gives older conversations a recovery path without making every line of chat text a file-discovery mechanism.

Load images when they become visible

A long history can contain many generated images. Loading all of them immediately would make reopening that history unnecessarily expensive.

The Vue component uses IntersectionObserver to begin reading images when their turn enters the viewport. It then reads each file through the desktop host's media interface.

Read or decode failures stay local to the affected image. The text answer and other previews remain usable. The large viewer uses the browser's native

element, with explicit controls for closing it.

The component is also keyed by session and turn so that switching conversations does not accidentally reuse another turn's media state.

What we verified

The release includes regression coverage for:

  • Artifact paths surviving save and load.
  • Legacy Code Mode output restoring the image metadata.
  • Plain strings, JSON strings, multiple lines, and duplicate paths.
  • Unrelated tools and failed steps being excluded from previews.
  • Single-image and multiple-image layouts, large-viewer controls, and local image errors.

The release notes record the full local check passing, 34 work-interface smoke checks, and 13 real-model scenarios passing with no failures or skips. The UI checks use fixtures to exercise display behavior; the real-model scenarios separately cover capabilities including image generation. Those are different kinds of evidence.

Try it or read the implementation

Download AIClaw 3.7.4.

The relevant code is small enough to follow directly:

  • Image preview component
  • Turn-level artifact selection
  • History compatibility logic
  • Persistence and compatibility tests

This feature previews local image artifacts produced by tools. Automatically recognizing arbitrary image URLs pasted into a conversation is a separate capability.

For an agent application, the saved conversation includes more than the assistant's words. Its outputs need enough structure to remain useful when the user returns later.

This post was prepared with AI assistance and checked against the AIClaw 3.7.4 implementation and release notes.
